magic-the-gathering.context_blurb: Magic: the Gathering is a trading card game — the very first one ever made — launched in August 1993 by a tiny company based in Renton, Washington, right across the lake from Seattle. Each player builds a custom deck from a huge pool of cards and duels another player by casting spells, summoning creatures, and paying the mana (magical energy) that lands produce, trying to reduce their opponent's twenty life points to zero. The game runs on five colors of mana, each with its own personality and tricks, and dozens of expansion sets have been printed over the decades. The earliest print runs from 1993 and 1994 are now treasured by collectors, with single rare cards from the first run selling for the price of a sports car. Magic kicked off the whole collectible-card craze that later swept up Pokemon and Yu-Gi-Oh!, and it remains the gold standard against which every later card game is measured. The lore around its early tournaments, misprints, and banned cards is a world unto itself, and the hobby's grognards remember the mid-1990s the way old wargamers remember the first boxes of Dungeons & Dragons. Many of its original designers and promoters came out of the Pacific Northwest's board-game and role-playing scene, and the stories of its first few years are legend among players.

pro-wrestling-wwf-wwe.context_blurb: Professional wrestling is scripted combat theater performed as a live athletic spectacle, and from the mid-1980s through the early 2000s the industry was ruled by two American companies: Vince McMahon's World Wrestling Federation (WWF, later renamed WWE) based in Connecticut, and Ted Turner's rival Atlanta-based World Championship Wrestling (WCW). The two companies fought a brutal ratings war on Monday nights in the 1990s, now remembered as the Monday Night Wars, trading champions, storylines, and famous match endings in a desperate scramble to keep fans. The era produced wrestling's biggest icons — larger-than-life characters who became household names, each with their own entrance music, catchphrase, costume, and signature finishing move. The companies ran a yearly calendar of huge pay-per-view spectacles, including the spring super-show that became the single biggest annual event in the whole industry, and the summer and winter stadium tours that ran alongside it. The infamous 1997 Montreal Screwjob incident is still argued about by fans today. Wrestling fans treat the specific finishing moves, catchphrases, and swerves of this period as sacred canon, and the Attitude Era in particular (roughly 1997-2002) is remembered as the medium's wildest, boldest commercial peak. Classic wrestling trivia almost always rewards someone who grew up watching cable TV at the right time. If you are curious about the medium, the real gateway is any of the big pay-per-views of the 1980s or the 1990s Monday Night Raw and Nitro episodes — they are the shows the whole industry's style was built on.

seattle-seahawks.context_blurb: The Seattle Seahawks are Seattle's National Football League (NFL) franchise, founded as a 1976 expansion team and based in Seattle, Washington. They play their home games indoors at Lumen Field (previously CenturyLink Field and Qwest Field) wearing navy, action green, and silver. For most of their history the franchise was middling, but a run of early-2010s teams built by their head coach of that era turned the team into a powerhouse — appearing in two Super Bowls back to back and famously winning Super Bowl XLVIII against the Denver Broncos in February 2014. That era's defense was so punishing that it earned its own fan nickname, and the team's star running back and quarterback both became household names. The franchise has given American football some of its loudest home-field advantages (crowd noise once registered as a small earthquake), one of its greatest wide receivers in the franchise's early years, and one of its most-second-guessed Super Bowl play calls. The players, coaches, Super Bowl moments, and Kingdome-era history are all part of the shared vocabulary of being a Pacific Northwest kid. For a Seattle sports fan, learning the two Super Bowl runs is a rite of passage, and old game footage of the playoff wins against the 49ers and the Saints is on YouTube and worth hunting down.

seattle-mariners.context_blurb: The Seattle Mariners are a Major League Baseball (MLB) team in the American League, founded as a 1977 expansion franchise and based in Seattle, Washington. They played their first decades indoors at the concrete Kingdome before moving in 1999 to the open-air Safeco Field (now T-Mobile Park). The 1990s and early 2000s were the franchise's golden age — a left-handed slugging center fielder with a gorgeous swing, a Japanese right fielder who revolutionized hitting after crossing the Pacific in 2001, a towering left-handed strikeout pitcher, and the beloved designated hitter whose number became a street name in Seattle. The 2001 Mariners tied an MLB record by winning 116 regular-season games, and the 1995 team gave the city one of the most legendary playoff moments in franchise history — a famous eleventh-inning hit scored from first base. The Mariners also hold a less happy record: the longest active postseason drought in North American pro sports stretched for most of the 2000s and 2010s. The catching tandem of father-and-son outfielders in 1990, perfect games, and the Kingdome-to-Safeco-to-T-Mobile transition are all part of the fabric of Mariners fandom. For a Seattle sports fan, the archive highlight reels of Griffey robbing home runs over the center-field wall and Ichiro's cannon arm from right field are both worth hunting down on YouTube — they capture something no written stat line can.

anime-dragon-ball.context_blurb: Dragon Ball is one of the most famous and influential Japanese manga and anime franchises of all time, created by Akira Toriyama. It started as a 1984 manga in Weekly Shonen Jump about a spiky-haired boy with a monkey tail who lives alone in the mountains and sets off to find seven magical orbs that, when gathered together, summon a wish-granting dragon. The story grew from a lighthearted martial-arts quest loosely inspired by the Chinese classic Journey to the West into the cosmic power-level epic Dragon Ball Z, which follows the grown-up hero and his friends as they defend Earth from alien tyrants and bio-engineered monsters. Toei Animation's anime adaptations aired in Japan starting in 1986 and later became huge American hits through Funimation's English dubs on Cartoon Network's Toonami block in the late 1990s. The franchise invented or popularized tropes — screamed power-up transformations, warrior training in weighted clothes, scouter-measured power levels, a sprawling cast of recurring fighters — that nearly every later shonen battle series has borrowed from. The spin-off Dragon Ball GT and the lightly-canon Dragon Ball Super continued the story, but the heart of the franchise is the original manga and the Z-era anime.

studio-ghibli.context_blurb: Studio Ghibli is a Japanese hand-drawn animation studio in Tokyo, founded in 1985 by two directors and their producer-partner after the success of a 1984 pre-Ghibli film about a wind-valley princess in a poisoned future world. The studio became famous worldwide for warm watercolor backgrounds, slow quiet pacing, flying scenes, impossibly detailed food, and stories centered on strong young girls encountering spirits, witches, forest gods, and talking animals. The studio's co-founding director directed the beloved films about two sisters finding a woodland spirit in rural Japan, a thirteen-year-old witch delivering packages in a European-styled town, a bathhouse of spirits in a hidden world, a wolf-raised girl and a cursed prince, and a wizard's walking castle. His quieter co-founder directed the heartbreaking wartime story of a brother and sister in 1945 Kobe and the reflective films that filled the studio's other half. Ghibli guards its hand-drawn style fiercely and has long resisted computer animation, and the studio became the gold standard against which almost every other animated feature is measured. In 1996 the studio signed a worldwide distribution deal with Disney, and Ghibli's films became permanent library titles in American and European homes. If you have never seen a Ghibli film, the easiest starting point is the gentle 1988 countryside story about two sisters — it is widely considered the perfect introduction to the whole studio's style.

neon-genesis-evangelion.context_blurb: Neon Genesis Evangelion is a 1995 Japanese anime series directed by Hideaki Anno at Studio Gainax, set in a near-future Tokyo under attack by huge geometric monsters called Angels that only three traumatized teenage pilots strapped inside towering biomechanical robots can stop. The show is set after a mysterious cataclysm called the Second Impact wiped out much of the world's population, and the surviving world is run by a shadowy UN-backed organization headquartered deep underground. What began as a mecha-robot action show gradually peeled away into one of the most psychologically unsettling anime ever made — the teenage pilots are depressed and lonely, the series is loaded with Jewish and Christian mythology used as striking visuals, and the famously bizarre ending split the plot action from the pilots' inner thoughts drawn in half-finished pencil sketches. Evangelion's merchandise and designs, especially the pale blue-haired pilot Rei Ayanami and the red-plug-suited Asuka, defined an entire era of Japanese pop culture and remain instantly recognizable decades later. The studio Gainax was founded by college-aged science-fiction fans who had broken through at a 1981 convention opening-ceremony short, and Evangelion was their all-in bet — Anno famously said he poured his own real depression into every frame of the show.

cowboy-bebop.context_blurb: Cowboy Bebop is a 1998 Japanese anime directed by Shinichiro Watanabe at Sunrise, about a scruffy crew of bounty hunters chasing criminals across the solar system in the year 2071 aboard a beaten-up ship called the Bebop. The main characters are a lanky ex-mob-syndicate hitman with a dark past, a gruff former cop with a prosthetic arm, a sly conwoman always chasing bigger scores, a weird genius hacker kid, and the smartest Welsh corgi in anime history. The show is famously stylish — jazz-noir cinematography, a world that mixes film-noir mood with westerns and 1970s cop shows — and its soundtrack by Yoko Kanno and her studio band is one of the most beloved in anime, blending jazz, blues, rock, bossa nova, and big-band swing. Cowboy Bebop first aired on TV Tokyo in 1998 and later ran uncut on Japan's satellite network WOWOW, then crossed to America on Cartoon Network's Adult Swim block in 2001, where it became many Western viewers' first serious adult anime. Its credit sequences, episode titles, and standalone single-episode stories are considered a high-water mark for what twenty-six-episode television can accomplish, and the series' quiet melancholy ending is often cited as one of the best in all of anime.

berserk.context_blurb: Berserk is a dark fantasy Japanese manga drawn by Kentaro Miura, who began it in 1988 and continued it almost without a pause until his sudden death in 2021 — leaving one of the longest, most feverishly detailed epics in the medium unfinished. Set in a medieval European-styled world of mercenaries, kings, and demons, it follows a huge scarred man wielding an impossibly oversized sword as he hunts down evil beings — hero and antihero both — through blood, trauma, and betrayal. The story's spine is a long flashback arc called the Golden Age, when the hero was still a hopeful young swordsman in the mercenary band of a charismatic beautiful commander with grand ambitions, and whose eventual betrayal (fans just call it the Eclipse) is one of the most infamous turning points in all of manga. Berserk's artwork — crosshatched, cathedral-dense, nightmarish — set the visual standard for dark fantasy, and its ideas have influenced everything from the Souls video games to a generation of later anime. Multiple anime adaptations exist: a 1997 TV series from OLM that covers the Golden Age arc, a trilogy of 2012-2013 films, and a controversial 2016-2017 CGI series. Fans generally agree the manga is the real work and the anime adaptations each have asterisks.

mobile-suit-gundam.context_blurb: Mobile Suit Gundam is a Japanese anime franchise created by director Yoshiyuki Tomino, launched in 1979 by Sunrise. It threw out the cartoon-style super-robot shows that had dominated 1970s Japanese TV and instead imagined giant piloted mechs — called mobile suits — as gritty military hardware, pulled on by sweating teenage soldiers in a sprawling war between Earth and the breakaway space colony state of Zeon. The original 1979 series flopped on first broadcast and was cut short by the network, but it exploded into a cultural phenomenon when Bandai released snap-together plastic kits — the famous Gunpla — letting kids build and paint the actual robots from the show. The franchise has run almost nonstop ever since, with new timelines, new wars, and dozens of spin-off series, films, and manga, including the 1995 series Gundam Wing that first conquered American TV through Cartoon Network's Toonami block, and the 2002 reboot Gundam SEED. Mobile Suit Gundam is treated by Japanese fans with reverence — the way American fans treat the original Star Wars trilogy. The original mobile-suit mechanical designs were drawn by Kunio Okawara, who essentially invented the visual grammar of serious anime mecha, and the franchise's models and model-kit lore are a whole hobby unto themselves.

akira.context_blurb: Akira is a 1988 Japanese animated science-fiction film directed by Katsuhiro Otomo, based on his own long-running manga. It opens with a huge silent blast leveling Tokyo in 1988 and jumps thirty years forward to 2019 Neo-Tokyo, a neon megacity built on top of the crater, where biker gangs fight in the streets and a secret military project studies psychic children. The film is considered a landmark of Japanese animation — Otomo demanded unprecedented detail, drew mouth movements to match the actors' recorded voices (reversing the industry norm), and used a huge budget to animate the kind of chase scenes most studios would have cut corners on. The soundtrack by the Japanese ensemble Geinoh Yamashirogumi blends taiko drums, Indonesian gamelan, and Noh chanting into one of the most unusual film scores ever made. When Akira finally opened in American theaters in late 1989, it introduced many Western viewers to the possibility that animated films could be serious, violent, and adult — and its red-bike shot and city skyline have been quoted by filmmakers ever since. The motorcycle-stop sequence alone has been imitated by Hollywood for decades, and the film's influence runs through films like The Matrix, Looper, and nearly every anime cyberpunk piece that followed.

ghost-in-the-shell.context_blurb: Ghost in the Shell is a Japanese cyberpunk manga by Masamune Shirow, first serialized in 1989, and the landmark 1995 anime film made at Production I.G. It is set in a near-future Hong Kong-style megacity where humans have progressively replaced their bodies with cybernetic parts and connect their brains directly to the Net — raising constant questions about where a person ends and a machine begins. The main character is a cybernetic police major leading an elite counter-terror unit of brain-and-body-augmented operatives, hunting a mysterious hacker called the Puppet Master through the city's data streams. Oshii's 1995 film was famously the first anime to systematically combine traditional cel animation with computer graphics for its glowing data streams and ghostly transparency effects, and the look of its rainy neon city has been quoted by nearly every live-action science-fiction film since — most obviously the Matrix trilogy, whose directors have openly cited it. The franchise has spawned sequel films, several TV series (including Stand Alone Complex), and endless debates about consciousness, identity, and what makes someone human. The elite unit's name — Public Security Section 9 — is one of the most quoted designations in cyberpunk. If you are curious about where cyberpunk visuals came from, the 1995 anime film is the single most-watched reference in the entire genre and is well worth tracking down.

rurouni-kenshin.context_blurb: Rurouni Kenshin is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Nobuhiro Watsuki from 1994 to 1999, with a popular 1996 anime from Studio Deen. It is set in Meiji-era Japan in the early 1870s, just after the samurai age officially ended and the country rushed into modernization. The main character is a wandering swordsman with a cross-shaped scar on his left cheek — a former imperial assassin from the civil war who has sworn never to kill again, and now carries a reverse-blade sword with its sharp edge facing himself. He takes up with a kind-hearted swordsmanship instructor at her Tokyo dojo and gets pulled into one government intrigue after another, meeting a cast of lively allies (a loudmouth brawler, a boy pickpocket, a woman doctor, a crafty swordsman-police captain) and tracking down former comrades-turned-villains from his assassin days. The anime adaptation ran into a common problem — the show caught up to the still-running manga — and Rurouni Kenshin has since generated several live-action film adaptations (starting in 2012) and manga sequels retelling the characters' later years. The Kyoto arc, following a scarred fire-wielding villain who plans to burn the new Meiji government to the ground, is widely considered the series' best.

trigun.context_blurb: Trigun is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Yasuhiro Nightow, first serialized in 1995, and the 1998 anime adaptation directed by Satoshi Nishimura at Madhouse. It is set on a dusty desert planet with two suns, settled generations ago by human colonists whose arriving ships crash-landed, leaving them scattered in little frontier towns. The main character is a tall, spiky-blond, red-coat-wearing gunfighter with the biggest bounty on his head anyone has ever seen — he carries a long silver revolver and leaves wrecked frontier towns in his wake, though he insists he is actually a kind pacifist who never kills. He gets dogged across the desert by a pair of insurance-company agents trying to prevent any more property damage, and he eventually finds his cold, dark-coated brother and a terrifying order of assassins who serve him. The anime's dusty cowboy-planet aesthetic blends spaghetti-western visuals with science-fiction worldbuilding, and the manga continued in a later run called Trigun Maximum after Nightow moved to a new publisher. The main character's over-the-top gunslinger iconography is a love letter to the Spaghetti Western — right down to his revolver design, which is modeled on real 1800s cap-and-ball guns. If you love cowboy shows, Trigun is the best anime gateway there is — the hero's over-the-top gunslinger stance has launched a thousand fan drawings.

slayers.context_blurb: Slayers is a comedy fantasy Japanese light novel series by Hajime Kanzaka, launched in 1989, with a long-running manga adaptation and a 1995 anime from studio J.C.Staff. It stars a short, red-haired, bad-tempered teenage sorceress with the biggest ego and the biggest destructive spell in the setting, as she wanders a traditional sword-and-sorcery world picking fights with bandits, dragons, and dark lords, usually for the loot. She teams up with a dim-witted blond swordsman, a priestess-fighter, and a chimera experiment of a man whose body is permanently stitched together from several creatures, and the group argues their way through fantasy quests full of exploding villages and bad puns. The anime series was a huge hit on Japanese TV in the 1990s and crossed to the United States in the early 2000s, and the main character's voice actress Megumi Hayashibara became one of the most-heard voice actresses in all of anime — she also voices Rei Ayanami in Neon Genesis Evangelion and Faye Valentine in Cowboy Bebop. Slayers helped define the comedy-fantasy genre for a whole generation of later series. It is one of the great gateway anime for kids who love Dungeons & Dragons. If you are starting out in anime, Slayers' silly tone and classic fantasy world make it one of the all-time best introductions to the medium.

lupin-iii.context_blurb: Lupin III is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Monkey Punch (Kazuhiko Kato), first serialized in 1967, and a long-running anime franchise that has produced TV series, films, and specials almost nonstop from the 1970s to today. The main character is a wisecracking master thief in a bright-colored jacket and skinny tie, said to be the grandson of the gentleman thief Arsene Lupin from the classic early-1900s French novels by Maurice Leblanc. He steals the world's most impossible treasures with a crew of regulars — a sharpshooter in a fedora and gray suit, a stoic samurai swordsman who can cut anything, and a shifty femme-fatale whose loyalties change by the paycheck — while being chased all over the globe by a determined Interpol detective. The 1979 film The Castle of Cagliostro, directed by Hayao Miyazaki (right before he co-founded Studio Ghibli), is widely considered one of the best in the franchise and features one of the most-copied animated car chases ever made — Steven Spielberg has reportedly called it one of the greatest action sequences in cinema. Lupin III is Japanese comfort-anime canon — a bit like James Bond crossed with the Pink Panther. If you have never seen one of the films, The Castle of Cagliostro is the universally recommended starting point in the whole franchise.

osamu-tezuka.context_blurb: Osamu Tezuka is the Japanese cartoonist widely called the 'God of Manga' — the founding figure who transformed Japanese comics from a kids' novelty into a serious storytelling medium. Born in 1928, Tezuka started drawing comics as a boy during World War II, went on to earn a medical degree while already becoming a working cartoonist, and in 1952 he began drawing a series about a bright-eyed robot boy built to look human after a brilliant scientist loses his real son — complete with rocket boots, machine guns in the hips, and lasers in the eyes. That character, Astro Boy, launched Tezuka's career and in 1963 became the first serialized Japanese TV anime, kicking off the whole industry that followed. Tezuka also drew the gender-bending Princess Knight, the medical thriller Black Jack, the lifelong-unfinished philosophical epic that he worked on for decades about an immortal firebird symbol of life, and the historical epic Buddha, among dozens of other series. He died in 1989, but his style — the big-eyed character design, the cinematic page layouts — set the visual grammar every later manga artist still works inside. Hayao Miyazaki famously admires Tezuka's manga while being critical of his anime, calling much of it rushed and cheap.

sailor-moon.context_blurb: Sailor Moon is a Japanese manga created by Naoko Takeuchi, serialized from 1991 to 1997, and the hit anime adaptation that aired on Japanese TV from 1992 to 1997. It stars a clumsy, cry-baby fourteen-year-old Tokyo schoolgirl who turns out to be the reincarnated princess of a lost ancient Moon Kingdom. She transforms into a magical warrior in a short sailor-suit costume with a tiara and heart-tipped weapons, and her teammates — teen girls named after the other planets in the solar system — each transform the same way to fight increasingly cosmic villains across five story arcs. Sailor Moon is widely considered the founding work of the modern 'magical girl' genre and the first global anime hit aimed squarely at girls, dubbed into dozens of languages and broadcast around the world. The American dub famously censored or rewrote entire relationships to fit 1990s network standards (making one lesbian couple into cousins, for instance), and the merchandise alone made Takeuchi one of the richest manga authors in Japanese history. The series has been remade twice as the more manga-faithful Sailor Moon Crystal (2014) and continues to anchor the international magical-girl fandom. If you are starting out, the original 1990s anime is widely available with subtitles today, and it holds up as one of the warmest coming-of-age magical-girl stories ever told.

my-hero-academia.context_blurb: My Hero Academia is a Japanese superhero manga written and drawn by Kohei Horikoshi, beginning in Weekly Shonen Jump in 2014. It is set in a world where almost every child is born with a superpower called a Quirk, and the strongest Quirk-users work as licensed professional heroes who fight villains for a living. The story follows a freckled, green-haired middle-schooler who was born without a Quirk at all, and his dream of attending the nation's top hero-training high school anyway. He catches the attention of the world's number-one hero — a towering, blond, super-muscular man whose famous grin is supposed to make everyone feel safe — and gets taken in as his secret successor. The anime adaptation from Bones studio has run from 2016 onward and has become one of the biggest shonen franchises of its generation. The series is loaded with named classmates, each with a distinctive Quirk, and a long rogue's gallery of villains built around a cracked-skin young leader with grudges against hero society. Be warned: the questions here give away major plot points.

hajime-no-ippo.context_blurb: Hajime no Ippo (literally 'The First Step') is a long-running Japanese boxing manga by George Morikawa — real name Jouji Morikawa — that began serialization in Weekly Shonen Magazine in 1989 and has continued for more than three decades. Three successive anime adaptations have run since 2000. The main character is a shy, mop-haired Japanese high-school boy who helps his widowed mother run her small coastal fishing-charter business. After getting beaten up by bullies and rescued by a passing professional boxer, the boy stumbles into a boxing gym in Tokyo and discovers he actually loves the sport. He is coached by a gruff retired champion and sparred by the gym's star fighters, slowly climbing from a shy amateur through the Japanese pro ranks and eventually toward world-title contenders. The series is considered one of the most technically detailed sports manga ever drawn — Morikawa studied real boxing gyms, cornerwork, training routines, and famous historical bouts to depict every punch — and its best bouts have become touchstones for anime boxing fans worldwide. Be warned: the questions here give away even the specific big-fight twists. If you are interested in boxing or in sports anime generally, the 2000-2002 Hajime no Ippo anime remains the single best gateway into the whole subgenre.

demon-slayer.context_blurb: Demon Slayer (in Japanese, Kimetsu no Yaiba) is a Japanese manga by Koyoharu Gotouge, serialized in Weekly Shonen Jump from 2016 to 2020 and adapted into a wildly popular anime by Tokyo studio Ufotable. The series is set in Japan's Taisho era, roughly the 1910s, in a world where flesh-eating demons prey on humans by night and a secret order of swordsmen called Demon Slayers hunts them down with specially forged black blades. The main character is a gentle young charcoal-seller who returns home from a trip to find his entire family slaughtered by a demon — except for his younger sister, who has survived but been turned partway into a demon herself. He straps her inside a wooden box and sets off to find a cure. The series is famous for Ufotable's dazzling animated swordfights — each slayer wields a unique Breathing Style named after natural forces like water, flame, or thunder — and the elite nine swordsmen called the Hashira. The 2020 anime film Mugen Train is one of the highest-grossing films in Japanese history. The ancient demon-king villain is a thousand-year-old polished nobleman who hides in plain sight in Tokyo and lords it over his twelve top demon lieutenants called the Twelve Kizuki, split into Upper and Lower ranks.

naruto.context_blurb: Naruto is a Japanese ninja manga written and drawn by Masashi Kishimoto, serialized in Weekly Shonen Jump from 1999 to 2014, with a Studio Pierrot anime adaptation that ran from 2002 and continued into the sequel series Naruto Shippuden through 2017. The main character is a loud, orange-jumpsuit-wearing, orphan ninja boy in the Hidden Leaf Village, who everyone treats as a troublemaker because he secretly carries a sealed nine-tailed demonic fox inside himself. He dreams of becoming the village's leader (the Hokage) one day, and climbs toward that goal through missions with his teammates — a brooding rival from an elite clan, a pink-haired classmate — under a lazy silver-haired teacher who hides his left eye under his headband. The series builds out an enormous world of ninja villages, forbidden techniques, legendary teachers (the Three Sannin), and a shadowy criminal organization called the Akatsuki that hunts tailed-beast hosts across the Shinobi World, culminating in a massive final world war. Naruto's mix of ninja action, found-family friendship, and signature spiraling-sphere technique turned it into one of the Big Three Weekly Shonen Jump franchises of its era alongside One Piece and Bleach. If you are starting out, the first few arcs of the anime are generally considered the best — the long filler stretches that come later test even hardcore fans.

one-piece.context_blurb: One Piece is a Japanese pirate manga written and drawn by Eiichiro Oda, serialized in Weekly Shonen Jump since July 1997, and the longest-running mega-hit in the magazine's history — now the bestselling manga series ever printed. The story follows a cheerful, straw-hat-wearing young pirate captain whose stretchy rubber body comes from eating a cursed Devil Fruit as a child, and his dream of sailing to the end of the ocean to find a legendary treasure left behind by the executed previous Pirate King. He gathers a crew of specialists — a green-haired three-sword swordsman, a blue-haired navigator, a sharpshooter, a lying cook, a reindeer doctor, an archaeologist, a cyborg shipwright, a skeleton musician — and sails one impossible-ocean island after another, building toward answers about a mysterious hundred-year gap in world history called the Void Century. One Piece has been adapted into a Toei Animation anime since 1999, a 2023 live-action Netflix series, and countless films — but Oda's long serialized manga, which he has promised an eventual ending to, is the heart of the franchise. The series' power system (Haki) and the three-type classification of Devil Fruits are among the most carefully worked out in all of shonen.

bleach.context_blurb: Bleach is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Tite Kubo, serialized in Weekly Shonen Jump from 2001 to 2016, with an anime adaptation from Studio Pierrot. The main character is an orange-haired Japanese high-school teenager who has always been able to see ghosts. One night a dark-robed Soul Reaper girl appears in his bedroom, chasing a monstrous ghost called a Hollow, and in the fight she is wounded and transfers her Soul Reaper powers to him. He is thrown into the duty of hunting Hollows and protecting souls, which drags him into the feudal-Japan-style Soul Society, an afterlife realm guarded by thirteen squads of elite captains. The series is built around huge, sweeping arcs — rescuing a captured ally from Soul Society execution, war against masked rogue captains in the realm of Hueco Mundo, and a final Thousand-Year Blood War against a soul-stealing ancient enemy — and every Soul Reaper wields a unique sealed sword called a zanpakuto with its own name and release command. Kubo's striking page compositions, sword-and-trenchcoat character designs, and nicknamed villains helped make Bleach one of the Big Three shonen manga of the 2000s alongside Naruto and One Piece. If you have never seen it, the opening Soul Society arc is widely considered the series' finest, and the Thousand-Year Blood War anime from 2022 onward has brought the final arc faithfully to screen.

attack-on-titan.context_blurb: Attack on Titan (in Japanese, Shingeki no Kyojin) is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Hajime Isayama, serialized from September 2009 through April 2021, with a hit anime adaptation that began on Wit Studio in 2013 and finished at MAPPA in 2023. The world of the story is a last remnant of humanity hiding behind three enormous concentric stone walls to protect itself from giant naked flesh-eating humanoids called Titans that roam the lands outside. When a mysterious colossal Titan suddenly kicks open the outer wall, Titans flood through, and three young friends — including the hot-tempered protagonist whose mother is killed in the attack — join the military and ultimately the dangerous Survey Corps unit that scouts beyond the walls. The series unfolds into an elaborate political saga about the real origins of the Titans, a buried thousand-year history of a people called the Eldians, and the moral collapse of its lead character — and its tone and finale are famously divisive among fans. The signature gear of the Survey Corps — the Omni-Directional Mobility Gear used to zip through forests and over Titan shoulders — is one of the most widely copied action-anime designs of its decade.

death-note.context_blurb: Death Note is a Japanese manga written by Tsugumi Ohba and drawn by Takeshi Obata, serialized in Weekly Shonen Jump from 2003 to 2006, with a Studio Madhouse anime adaptation in 2006-2007. The main character is a brilliant, bored Japanese high-school student in Tokyo who picks up a black leather notebook dropped by a bored god of death. Any human whose name is written in the notebook — while the writer is picturing that specific person's face — dies, by default of a heart attack within forty seconds. The student decides to use it to secretly kill criminals around the world, convinced he is purifying humanity and will become the god of the new era. The world's police respond by recruiting a reclusive, crouched, sugar-addicted genius detective to hunt the killer, and the series becomes a long cat-and-mouse battle of wits fought almost entirely in rooms of surveillance monitors, half-truths, trap-and-counter-trap setups, and televised bluffs. It is widely considered one of the sharpest psychological thrillers in all of manga, and the Obata art — particularly the way the detective sits crouched on his heels while thinking — has defined the visual vocabulary of a whole generation of later series. If you love mystery or psychological thrillers, Death Note is one of the two or three most universally recommended gateway anime ever made.

fullmetal-alchemist.context_blurb: Fullmetal Alchemist is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Hiromu Arakawa, serialized from 2001 to 2010, with two anime adaptations — the first in 2003-2004 (which ran past the manga and invented its own ending) and the fan-preferred 2009-2010 Brotherhood that follows the manga faithfully. It is set in a fictional country modeled on 1900s Europe called Amestris, in a world where the science of alchemy — rearranging matter through drawn transmutation circles — is real but strictly obeys a law of equivalent exchange. Two young brothers try to use alchemy to resurrect their dead mother, pay a horrifying price when the ritual rebounds, and set out across the country to find the legendary Philosopher's Stone that might reverse the damage. Along the way they are drawn into a vast state conspiracy involving a group of seven artificial beings named after the Christian deadly sins and ruled by an ancient homunculus called Father, whose plans for the whole country unfold against a painted backdrop of military politics, war guilt, and family bonds. Arakawa — originally a Hokkaido farm kid — poured a serious moral and theological weight into the series that fans still rank among the best in all of shonen manga.

hunter-x-hunter.context_blurb: Hunter x Hunter is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Yoshihiro Togashi, serialized in Weekly Shonen Jump since 1998 — though the author's chronic back pain has forced multiple extended hiatuses stretching years at a time. The main character is a cheerful green-haired twelve-year-old boy raised by his aunt on a tiny island, who learns that the father he never knew is actually a legendary member of a secretive licensed profession called Hunters, and sets off to take the brutal multi-stage Hunter Exam himself. Among the applicants he meets a lanky blond kid studying to become a doctor, a stiff angry teen seeking revenge for his murdered clan, and a soft-spoken white-haired boy who turns out to be the twelve-year-old heir of the world's most famous assassin family. The series has moved through long distinct arcs — the Hunter Exam, Heavens Arena, Yorknew City, Greed Island, the Chimera Ant invasion, and the current Dark Continent plot — and treats its battle system of personalized aura abilities called Nen as one of the most carefully worked-out power systems in all of shonen. Hunter x Hunter is a long game for patient readers — a deep cut that devoted manga fans prize.

jojos-bizarre-adventure.context_blurb: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Hirohiko Araki, serialized almost continuously since 1987 across nine numbered Parts in two Shueisha magazines — one of the longest and most ambitious manga runs in the medium. Each Part is set in a different era (Victorian England, 1930s Egypt, 1980s Japan, 1990s small-town Japan, 2001 Italy, modern Florida) and stars a new member of the Joestar bloodline, who is always known by a nickname that reduces his first name to the two syllables 'JoJo.' Across generations, the Joestars battle supernatural threats — originally a vampire ancestor turned villain, then stand-wielding assassins, then a serial killer in a quiet town, then the Italian mafia. From Part 3 onward, the manga introduced its signature mechanic: fighters wield 'Stands,' invisible-except-to-other-Stand-users spirit companions with individual names (nearly all borrowed from classic rock songs and albums) and bizarre specific powers. Araki's art style — huge muscles, dramatic 1980s fashion-magazine poses — is as iconic as the plots themselves, and the series' catchphrases, menacing-stance panels, and specific Stand ability reveals are endlessly meme-able online. For a new reader, the chronological starting point is 1987's Phantom Blood, but most fans recommend jumping straight into Part 3's 1988 Egypt road trip as the real gateway. The 2012-onward anime adaptation covers the whole saga in rolling batches.

yu-yu-hakusho.context_blurb: Yu Yu Hakusho (literally 'Ghost Files') is a Japanese manga written and drawn by Yoshihiro Togashi, serialized in Weekly Shonen Jump from 1990 to 1994 and adapted into a 1992-1995 anime by Studio Pierrot. The main character is a tough middle-school delinquent with a black slicked-back pompadour who skips class, brawls, and gambles — until one afternoon he dies while pushing a child out of the path of a speeding car. His selfless death surprises the afterlife, and he is given a chance to come back to life if he will work as a Spirit Detective, policing supernatural threats to the human world. He teams up with a short, white-forelocked demon swordsman, a tall red-haired fox-demon, and his old brawling rival, and the series climaxes in a long arena-tournament arc called the Dark Tournament. Togashi developed the back problems that have slowed Hunter x Hunter for decades during this run, and the series' late arcs ended abruptly as a result. Yu Yu Hakusho was one of the earliest big anime hits to reach American kids on Cartoon Network's Toonami block, where its stylish fights and 90s-shonen aesthetic made it a gateway anime for an entire generation. If you are starting out, the big tournament arc is widely considered the series' peak and is where many fans point newcomers first.

initial-d.context_blurb: Initial D is a Japanese street-racing manga written and drawn by Shuichi Shigeno, serialized in Young Magazine from 1995 to 2013, with a popular 1998 anime adaptation. It is set in the mountains of Gunma Prefecture, Japan, in the 1990s, in a world of late-night downhill touge races on twisty two-lane roads, where small teams of young drivers push their modified cars sideways through hairpin corners at terrifying speed. The main character is a quiet high-school boy who makes nightly tofu-delivery runs down the mountain in his father's beat-up ten-year-old Toyota — unaware that his father, a legendary former touge driver, has been secretly training him into the fastest downhill driver in the prefecture. The series is built around genuine real-world roads, real production-car models, and specific real tuning parts, and the anime made Japan's mountain-pass drifting culture a global phenomenon. Its soundtrack of imported Italian Eurobeat became as recognizable as the series itself. Initial D is foundational canon for the whole modern car-and-anime fandom, and specific driver skills — hand brakes, feint motions, gutter runs — are part of the shared vocabulary. If you like cars, Initial D is the best anime gateway there is — the opening episodes include nighttime drift sequences that have launched a whole generation of real-world car hobbyists.

toilet-bound-hanako-kun.context_blurb: Toilet-Bound Hanako-kun (in Japanese, Jibaku Shonen Hanako-kun) is a Japanese supernatural comedy manga written and drawn by the duo Aida Iro, serialized since 2014, with a popular 2020 anime adaptation from studio Lerche. It is set at Kamome Academy, a Japanese high school famous for its Seven Mysteries — ghost stories whispered by students that have turned out to be real resident spirits with their own rules and territories. The protagonist is a shy, superstitious first-year girl who summons a charming boy ghost rumored to haunt the third stall of the old girls' bathroom on the third floor. She asks him for a love potion, accidentally becomes bound to his service, and gets pulled into one strange hauntings-and-mysteries case after another, meeting the other six supernaturals and uncovering the boy ghost's melancholy history, including a mysterious twin brother. The anime is immediately recognizable for its soft pastel watercolor-and-chalk visual style and dreamy Lerche art direction. Be warned: the questions here give away even the deeper reveals about the ghost's past and his twin. If you are starting out, the 2020 anime is widely available with subtitles today and runs through roughly the manga's first six volumes in twelve episodes.

anime-misc-classics.context_blurb: Here is a cluster of beloved Japanese manga and anime classics. It includes Kazuki Takahashi's 1996 trading-card battle series, set in a world where a shy high-school boy plays a cardboard duel game designed by his grandfather; Rumiko Takahashi's 1996 feudal-era fantasy, where a modern Japanese schoolgirl falls down a shrine well into Japan's past; Yoichi Takahashi's long-running soccer manga Captain Tsubasa (1981), credited with inspiring real-world professional soccer stars; Buronson and Tetsuo Hara's post-apocalyptic martial-arts epic Fist of the North Star (1983); Sunrise's 2006 schemer-prince mecha series Code Geass; Studio Gainax's wild six-episode 2000 anime FLCL ('Fooly Cooly'); Shinichiro Watanabe's hip-hop-scored samurai road-trip series Samurai Champloo (2004); Yuki Urushibara's quiet dreamlike anime Mushishi (2005); Akira Toriyama's gag-comedy manga Dr. Slump (1980); the Bandai virtual-pet-turned-anime phenomenon Digimon (1997); and Takehiko Inoue's cult basketball manga Slam Dunk (1990). Each of these is a classic in its own right and worth seeking out. Each of these series has its own passionate fandom, and tracking down the originals is part of the fun of being an anime geek.

princess-bride.context_blurb: The Princess Bride is a 1987 American fantasy comedy film directed by Rob Reiner and written by William Goldman — adapted from Goldman's own 1973 fantasy novel of the same name, which is itself famously framed as the 'abridgement' of a much longer work by a fictional author named S. Morgenstern. The movie is told as a bedtime story, with a grandfather (Peter Falk) reading to his sick grandson (a young Fred Savage), about a poor farm boy named Westley who falls in love with a beautiful farm girl named Buttercup, loses her to pirates, and comes back years later disguised as a mysterious masked swordsman to rescue her from an evil prince's wedding. The cast is a who's-who of 1980s talent: Cary Elwes as Westley, Robin Wright as Buttercup, Mandy Patinkin as the Spanish swordsman Inigo Montoya seeking vengeance for his father, the French giant Andre the Giant as the friendly brute Fezzik, Wallace Shawn as a bald loudmouth Sicilian mastermind, Billy Crystal and Carol Kane as a bickering old miracle-maker couple. It is one of the most quotable comedies ever made and its plot has passed into common knowledge. Many kids have had the whole script memorized since fourth grade.

back-to-the-future.context_blurb: Back to the Future is an American science-fiction comedy film trilogy directed by Robert Zemeckis and co-written with Bob Gale, produced by Steven Spielberg's Amblin Entertainment. The first film came out in 1985 and starred Michael J. Fox as a California teenage skateboarder in 1985 whose eccentric scientist friend, Dr. Emmett 'Doc' Brown (Christopher Lloyd), has built a working time machine out of a stainless-steel sports car. The teenager accidentally travels back to 1955, almost erases his own existence by interrupting his parents' meeting, and has to repair the timeline before he fades out of a Polaroid photo of himself and his siblings. Back to the Future Part II (1989) sends the heroes forward to a wild predicted 2015, and Part III (1990) throws them back to 1885 Hill Valley in the Wild West. The trilogy is beloved for its clockwork plotting, Alan Silvestri's rousing orchestral score, and its two leads' chemistry, and it has been quoted by nearly every time-travel movie made since. Doc Brown's catchphrase of surprise and the DeLorean's famous time-travel speed have both passed deep into American pop-culture vocabulary. If you have never seen the films, the 1985 original is the right starting point — the sequels only make full sense after seeing it.

ghostbusters.context_blurb: Ghostbusters is a 1984 American supernatural comedy film directed by Ivan Reitman and written by its stars, Dan Aykroyd and Harold Ramis. It follows three New York City parapsychology professors — played by Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, and Harold Ramis — who get fired from Columbia University and launch a private commercial ghost-exterminating business out of a disused firehouse in Manhattan, hiring a working-class fourth member along the way. They catch rising numbers of ghosts in the city with proton-pack-and-trap tech of their own invention, culminating in a huge rooftop battle with a Sumerian god who manifests above the city as a terrifying giant marshmallow mascot. The film was shot on a $30 million budget, became the highest-grossing comedy of 1984, and its Ray Parker Jr. theme song became one of the biggest hits of the decade (and the subject of a famous lawsuit from Huey Lewis). A 1989 sequel followed, along with a 1986 Saturday-morning cartoon series called The Real Ghostbusters and later reboots and legacy sequels, but the original 1984 film is the one everyone quotes. Dan Aykroyd famously originally wrote the script for a very different team including John Belushi, before Belushi's 1982 death forced a rewrite.

scott-pilgrim.context_blurb: Scott Pilgrim is a six-volume black-and-white Canadian graphic novel series written and drawn by Bryan Lee O'Malley, published from 2004 to 2010, and adapted into the 2010 live-action film Scott Pilgrim vs. the World, directed by British filmmaker Edgar Wright and starring Michael Cera. The series is set in Toronto, Canada, and follows a broke 23-year-old bass player in a struggling indie rock band who falls for a mysterious American delivery girl with constantly-changing hair color — only to discover that in order to date her he has to defeat her seven evil exes in literal video-game-style combat, complete with floating pixel-art hit points, coins, extra lives, and power-ups. The books and film treat the whole twenty-something Toronto music-scene milieu as a video game come to life, loaded with references to Super Mario Bros., The Legend of Zelda, Street Fighter II, Final Fantasy, and dozens of other classics. The 2010 film was a financial disappointment on release but has since become a huge cult favorite, and a 2023 anime series adapted the full comic story on Netflix with the original movie cast returning as voice actors. Be warned: the questions here give away the plot. If you grew up on classic video games, Scott Pilgrim is almost designed as a gift — every page and scene is a reference to a classic game or band.

super-mario-bros-movie-2023.context_blurb: The Super Mario Bros. Movie is a 2023 animated feature film produced by Illumination and Nintendo, based on Nintendo's Super Mario Bros. video-game series. It made over one billion dollars at the global box office. The film opens in Brooklyn, New York, where the Italian-American plumber brothers Mario (voiced by Chris Pratt) and Luigi (Charlie Day) have just launched their own plumbing business and get sucked through a city sewer pipe into the fantastical Mushroom Kingdom. Mario meets its ruler, Princess Peach, who is defending her kingdom from the invading koopa king Bowser (voiced by Jack Black) and his massive army. Mario trains to fight back, picks up his signature power-ups, teams up with Donkey Kong and the Kong tribe, and races to rescue his captured brother. The film is loaded with deep-cut references for players of the Nintendo games — specific levels, specific power-ups, specific musical cues from the 1985 original and later entries — and plays as a love letter to classic Nintendo. Be warned: the questions here give away the plot of the 2023 film. Jack Black's piano ballad from the film became an unexpected real-world top-forty radio hit.

terminator-franchise.context_blurb: The Terminator is an American science-fiction action film franchise created by Canadian director James Cameron, who conceived the first script in the early 1980s and famously sold it to a producer for one dollar on the condition that he would get to direct it himself. The 1984 original stars Arnold Schwarzenegger as a killer cyborg sent back from a dystopian post-nuclear-war future, hunting a Los Angeles waitress whose unborn son will one day lead humanity's resistance against the machines. The 1991 sequel Terminator 2: Judgment Day flips the formula — Schwarzenegger's model is now a reprogrammed protector guarding the waitress's teenage son against a far more advanced shape-shifting liquid-metal cyborg. T2 was one of the first blockbusters to lean heavily on computer-generated imagery (CGI), with Industrial Light & Magic developing custom morphing software for the liquid-metal effects. The franchise has produced several later sequels and TV spinoffs that fans debate, but the first two Cameron films are the canonical pair — and Schwarzenegger's two-word tagline from the 1984 original has become one of the most-quoted lines in cinema. His casting is itself legend — Cameron originally considered giving him a different lead role in the film. If you are starting out, the 1984 original and 1991 sequel are the two to see — in that order — before any of the later entries.

karate-kid.context_blurb: The Karate Kid is a 1984 American martial-arts drama film directed by John G. Avildsen (who had already won a Best Director Oscar for the 1976 boxing film Rocky) and starring Ralph Macchio as the teenage protagonist Daniel LaRusso. The story opens with Daniel moving with his widowed mother from New Jersey to Reseda in southern California, where he quickly becomes the bullying target of a gang of boys from a cruel local karate dojo called Cobra Kai. He is secretly taken under the wing of his apartment building's gentle Japanese-American handyman Mr. Miyagi (played by Pat Morita, whose own real backstory echoes Miyagi's wartime scenes), who trains him in Okinawan karate through chore-based muscle-memory drills — waxing cars, painting fences, sanding decks — and prepares him to defeat the bullies at the All-Valley Karate Tournament. The film built the whole 'wise mentor and unlikely-student' sports-drama template, launched a 1980s franchise of sequels, and inspired the long-running sequel streaming series Cobra Kai starting in 2018. Specific moves and lines from the tournament sequence have been quoted and parodied by nearly every sports film made since. If you are interested in martial arts or in classic sports films, The Karate Kid is widely considered the best 1980s starting point there is.

top-gun.context_blurb: Top Gun is a 1986 American aerial-combat drama directed by Tony Scott (the younger brother of Ridley Scott), produced by Don Simpson and Jerry Bruckheimer, and starring Tom Cruise. The film opens with a cocky young U.S. Naval fighter aviator named Pete Mitchell being accepted into the elite fighter-weapons school at Naval Air Station Miramar in southern California — the real Navy school known in the Pentagon as 'Top Gun' — alongside his back-seater and his hotshot rival pilots. Mitchell flies the F-14 Tomcat, pulls high-speed maneuvers around aircraft carriers, falls for a civilian flight instructor played by Kelly McGillis, and lives through a mid-air disaster that forces him to decide whether he still wants to fly. The film was shot on a budget that was unusually high for a non-effects-driven movie at the time, with the U.S. Navy loaning actual F-14s and carriers for filming. It became the highest-grossing film of 1986, launched Cruise's career as an action star, and its Kenny Loggins theme song 'Danger Zone' became one of the most iconic needle-drops in cinema. A 2022 legacy sequel starring Cruise, Top Gun: Maverick, followed thirty-six years later. If you are interested in military aviation or in classic 1980s action, Top Gun is foundational viewing — and the 2022 sequel is the rare legacy follow-up most fans agree improves on the original.

the-goonies.context_blurb: The Goonies is a 1985 American kids-adventure film directed by Richard Donner (who had already made The Omen in 1976 and Superman in 1978), produced by Steven Spielberg, and written by Chris Columbus from a story Spielberg sketched out. The film is set in Astoria, Oregon, in the real coastal Pacific Northwest. A gang of middle-school friends living in a neighborhood called the Goon Docks are about to lose their homes to a developer bulldozing them for a country-club golf course. In the family attic, the asthmatic protagonist Mikey (played by a young Sean Astin, who would later play Samwise Gamgee in the Lord of the Rings films) and his friends find a 300-year-old treasure map pointing to a pirate's buried fortune hidden in a cave network beneath their town. They sneak off to find it, pursued by a comic trio of criminal fugitives. The film also features Josh Brolin, Corey Feldman, Jonathan Ke Quan, and a huge beloved monster-ally called Sloth, and its Cyndi Lauper theme song was a hit single. It remains the defining Spielberg-era kids'-treasure-hunt movie, and specific scenes — the Fratelli family hideout, the pirate ship, the 'truffle shuffle' — are part of the shared childhood vocabulary of several generations.

et-the-extra-terrestrial.context_blurb: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial is a 1982 American science-fiction family film directed by Steven Spielberg, written by Melissa Mathison, and starring a cast of child actors including Henry Thomas and a seven-year-old Drew Barrymore. The story opens in a quiet California suburb where a sweet, big-eyed, three-foot-tall alien is accidentally left behind by his departing spaceship and takes refuge in a lonely boy's backyard tool shed. The boy, Elliott, befriends the alien, hides him in his bedroom, and slowly reveals him to his younger sister and older brother while a government agency closes in. Together they build a makeshift communications rig to help the alien 'phone home.' The film became the highest-grossing of its era, revolutionized Hollywood merchandising around a non-sequel movie, and gave American cinema one of its most-quoted silhouettes — a boy and an alien on a bicycle flying across a full moon. The score by John Williams is one of his most beloved, and the specific movie-tie-in candy deal around the film became an industry-defining case study in product placement — Mars Inc. famously turned the deal down and a rival candy brand's sales tripled after the movie opened. If you have never seen E.T., it holds up decades later as one of the most beloved family films ever made.

indiana-jones.context_blurb: Indiana Jones is an American adventure film franchise created by George Lucas and Steven Spielberg, launched in 1981 with Raiders of the Lost Ark. Harrison Ford stars as Dr. Henry 'Indiana' Jones Jr., a globe-trotting archaeology professor who divides his life between classroom lectures and whip-cracking, bull-whip-wielding, Nazi-fighting treasure hunts for ancient religious artifacts, wearing his iconic brown leather jacket and brown wide-brimmed hat. Raiders (1981) sends him racing the Nazis to the Ark of the Covenant in 1936 Egypt and Nepal; the darker 1984 prequel Temple of Doom pits him against a Thuggee death-cult in India with a spunky Chinese-American kid sidekick named Short Round (played by a young Jonathan Ke Quan); and the 1989 Last Crusade teams Indy with his crusty medievalist father (played by Sean Connery, in a part Spielberg conceived to evoke 'James Bond as the father of Indiana Jones') on a hunt for the Holy Grail in Petra, Jordan. Two later entries followed, but the original 1981-1989 trilogy is the canonical heart of the series — a pulp-magazine-inspired, Saturday-matinee love letter that defined blockbuster adventure for the whole 1980s. If you have never seen the films, the 1981 original is the right starting point — it is still widely regarded as the best action-adventure movie ever made.

schwarzenegger-80s-action.context_blurb: Arnold Schwarzenegger's action films defined 1980s and early-1990s American blockbuster cinema, even with the Terminator films set aside. The three big ones here are John Milius's 1982 fantasy Conan the Barbarian, in which Schwarzenegger plays Robert E. Howard's muscular Cimmerian wandering warrior Conan hunting a snake-cult wizard named Thulsa Doom (played by James Earl Jones) who murdered his parents; John McTiernan's 1987 jungle sci-fi-horror Predator, in which Schwarzenegger leads a special-forces team being picked off one by one by an invisible alien trophy-hunter in a Central American jungle; and Paul Verhoeven's 1990 Mars-based thriller Total Recall, in which Schwarzenegger plays a construction worker whose implanted vacation memories either are or are not fake. All three were shaped by their towering, Austrian-accented leading man and by the practical-effects and jungle-shooting conditions of their era, and all three leaned hard into huge-weapon action, memorable one-liners, and physical sets rather than later-era digital effects. Basil Poledouris's choral-and-anvil score for Conan the Barbarian is one of the most imitated fantasy soundtracks ever recorded. If you are curious about the whole 1980s action-film era, these three films together give a complete tour of what Schwarzenegger meant to the decade.

alien-franchise.context_blurb: Alien is an American science-fiction horror film franchise launched in 1979 with Ridley Scott's Alien, in which the crew of the deep-space towing ship Nostromo answers a distress signal, picks up a nightmare parasitic creature designed by the Swiss surrealist painter H.R. Giger, and is systematically killed off until only one warrant officer (played by Sigourney Weaver) and the ship's cat survive. The 1986 sequel Aliens, directed by James Cameron, flipped the tone from haunted-house horror to military action: Ripley wakes up from decades of frozen sleep and joins a squad of Colonial Marines heading back to the planet LV-426 to find the nightmare has become an infestation. Aliens introduced the badass powered-exoskeleton forklift fight, the squad of memorable grunts, and the little girl Newt whom Ripley adopts across the course of the film. The original 1979 and 1986 films are the canonical pair; later entries (Alien 3, Alien Resurrection, Prometheus, Alien: Covenant, Romulus) continue the series with varying reputations among fans. Both of the original films were marketing landmarks — the 1979 original was sold with the tagline 'In space, no one can hear you scream,' one of the most famous in cinema history. If you have never seen them, the 1979 original and 1986 sequel work beautifully as a horror-and-action double feature — different in tone but equally brilliant.

star-wars-original-trilogy.context_blurb: The original Star Wars trilogy is three American science-fantasy films — A New Hope (1977), The Empire Strikes Back (1980), and Return of the Jedi (1983) — written by George Lucas, produced by his company Lucasfilm, and distributed by 20th Century Fox. The story is set in a galaxy far, far away, in an ongoing war between the authoritarian Galactic Empire and the Rebel Alliance that is trying to overthrow it. In A New Hope, a farmboy named Luke Skywalker living on a desert planet with two suns receives a hidden message from a princess being held captive aboard the Empire's planet-destroying battle station, is trained briefly by an old hermit knight in the mystical energy field called the Force, and joins up with a smuggler, a Wookiee, and two droids to attack the station. The Empire Strikes Back introduces the swamp-dwelling little green Jedi Master Yoda and ends on the most famous family-reveal twist in cinema history. The main plot beats of these three films have crossed into universal common knowledge. The 1977 original was scored by John Williams and performed by the London Symphony Orchestra, a choice that reshaped Hollywood film music for decades.

tombstone-wyatt-earp.context_blurb: Tombstone is a 1993 American Western film directed by George P. Cosmatos (though the film's chaotic production has been widely credited to star Kurt Russell doing much of the actual directing) and starring Russell as Marshal Wyatt Earp and Val Kilmer in a career-defining supporting turn as the gambler, dentist, and lethal gunfighter 'Doc' Holliday — John Henry Holliday, who was dying of tuberculosis in real life throughout the events depicted. The film dramatizes real historical events in 1881 Arizona Territory: the Earp brothers (Wyatt, Virgil, Morgan) and Doc Holliday arrive in the silver-mining boomtown of Tombstone, clash with a loose gang of cattle rustlers known as the Cowboys, fight the thirty-second October 26 shootout at the O.K. Corral vacant lot that made them legends, and ride out the Vendetta Ride after one of the brothers is killed. The screenplay was written by Kevin Jarre, who also wrote the Civil War film Glory. The real Wyatt Earp lived decades longer, befriended early Hollywood cowboy stars Tom Mix and a young John Wayne, and died in Los Angeles in 1929. The real Doc Holliday died of tuberculosis in Glenwood Springs, Colorado in November 1887. If you are interested in American history or in classic Westerns, Tombstone is one of the great gateway films — Val Kilmer's performance alone is reason to see it.

blade-runner.context_blurb: Blade Runner is a 1982 American science-fiction film directed by British filmmaker Ridley Scott and loosely adapted from a 1968 novel by the American science-fiction writer Philip K. Dick. It stars Harrison Ford as Rick Deckard, a burnt-out ex-police detective working in a dense, rainy, neon-drenched 2019 Los Angeles. His job (he's a 'blade runner') is to track down and 'retire' a small group of escaped bio-engineered humans who have returned illegally to Earth, led by an extraordinary blond fugitive named Roy Batty (played by Rutger Hauer). The film is famous for its wet-neon production design that defined cyberpunk visual language, its dreamy electronic score by the Greek composer Vangelis performed on his Yamaha CS-80 synthesizer, and the climactic rooftop monologue Hauer rewrote the night before shooting in his hotel room. Blade Runner opened poorly in 1982 to a chilly box office — partly because it opened against E.T. — but became one of the most influential science-fiction films ever made, with a 2017 sequel following three and a half decades later. The film's troubled theatrical release and multiple director's-cut versions are themselves a famous film-history story. If you are curious about where cyberpunk comes from, this is the single most-watched reference film in the whole visual tradition — track down the Final Cut if possible.

don-bluth.context_blurb: Don Bluth is an American animator who worked at Walt Disney Animation Studios from 1955 to 1979, then famously quit on September 13, 1979, taking a group of other senior Disney artists with him — angry that the Disney studio was increasingly using the xerography shortcut to cheapen its animation process. Bluth and his colleagues founded their own studio and launched a run of beloved 1980s hand-drawn animated features that competed directly with Disney's much weaker output of that decade. The signature Bluth films are: the 1982 fantasy The Secret of NIMH (based on Robert C. O'Brien's 1971 children's novel about rats enhanced by lab experiments); the 1986 Steven Spielberg-produced immigration tale An American Tail, following a Russian-Jewish mouse named Fievel fleeing the 1881-1884 Russian pogroms; the 1988 dinosaur-journey film The Land Before Time, also with Spielberg; the 1989 All Dogs Go to Heaven, which released against Disney's The Little Mermaid; and the 1983 full-cel-animated laserdisc arcade game Dragon's Lair, which Bluth drew for Cinematronics and which looked like no other arcade machine of its era. Bluth's influence on 1980s animation and the resurgence of hand-drawn adventure films is a story every animation nerd knows cold. If you are interested in animation history, Bluth's departure from Disney in 1979 is one of the foundational stories of the whole modern industry.

westerns-and-old-west-lore.context_blurb: The classic American Western film genre grew out of the real historical Old West figures who inspired it. The best-known 1930s-1960s Western film star was John Wayne, born Marion Robert Morrison in Winterset, Iowa in 1907, who starred in dozens of films by director John Ford including the 1939 breakthrough Stagecoach and the 1956 masterpiece The Searchers, both filmed in Monument Valley on the Arizona-Utah border. In the 1960s the Italian director Sergio Leone reinvented the genre with his three 'Dollars' films starring American actor Clint Eastwood as the Man with No Name — A Fistful of Dollars, For a Few Dollars More, and the three-way-standoff epic The Good, the Bad and the Ugly — followed by the sweeping 1968 Once Upon a Time in the West. The real figures the films draw on include the lawman Wyatt Earp, his tuberculosis-ridden dentist friend Doc Holliday, the gunfighters Wild Bill Hickok (shot dead in Deadwood holding aces-and-eights in 1876) and Jesse James, the outlaw Billy the Kid of New Mexico Territory's Lincoln County War, the outlaw-pair Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, and Buffalo Bill Cody's touring 1883-1913 Wild West Show. Later Westerns include Clint Eastwood's 1985 Pale Rider, his 1992 Oscar-winning Unforgiven, and Kevin Costner's 1990 Dances with Wolves, as well as the 1960 American remake The Magnificent Seven (adapted from a 1954 Akira Kurosawa epic).

saturday-morning-cartoons.context_blurb: The beloved Saturday-morning and after-school American animated TV cartoons of the 1980s and 1990s were a golden age, when every kid grew up on the same shared pool of talking turtles, transforming robots, mythic warriors, cereal commercials, and giant mega-robots. The 1980s wave was driven by toy companies partnering with animation studios like Filmation, Hanna-Barbera, and Rankin/Bass to launch half-hour cartoons tied to action-figure lines: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (1987), ThunderCats (1985), the Transformers (1984), G.I. Joe: A Real American Hero (1985), He-Man and the Masters of the Universe (1983), She-Ra: Princess of Power (1985), Voltron (1984), Inspector Gadget (1983), M.A.S.K. (1985), SilverHawks (1986), and BraveStarr (1987). Disney launched its Afternoon syndicated block (DuckTales 1987, Darkwing Duck 1991, TaleSpin 1990, Gargoyles 1994). Warner Bros. revived its characters with Tiny Toon Adventures (1990), Animaniacs (1993), Freakazoid! (1995), and the landmark Batman: The Animated Series (1992). Fox Kids ran the hugely successful X-Men animated series starting in 1992, Spider-Man in 1994, and Nickelodeon launched its own line (Rugrats 1991, The Ren & Stimpy Show 1991, Doug 1991, Hey Arnold! 1996, Recess 1997). Captain Planet (1990) added environmental messaging to the mix, and the Looney Tunes continued to run across decades of reruns.

christmas-and-holiday-specials.context_blurb: The beloved American Christmas and Halloween holiday films and television specials are the kinds that families watch every year and that have passed into shared cultural knowledge. The Christmas specials include the 1965 CBS Peanuts special A Charlie Brown Christmas (based on Charles Schulz's Peanuts comic strip, with its jazz-piano score and Linus's Luke 2 reading); the stop-motion Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer (1964), Santa Claus Is Comin' to Town (1970), and The Year Without a Santa Claus (1974); the 1983 live-action A Christmas Story (set in 1940s Indiana, about a boy who wants one specific gift); the 1989 National Lampoon's Christmas Vacation, with its hapless suburban dad Clark Griswold; the 1990 Home Alone starring Macaulay Culkin as an eight-year-old accidentally left behind by his family; the 2003 Will Ferrell comedy Elf; the 2004 Robert Zemeckis motion-capture film The Polar Express; and the 1988 John McTiernan action film Die Hard, whose status as a Christmas movie is the subject of eternal online debate. The 1993 Tim Burton-produced stop-motion film The Nightmare Before Christmas crosses between Halloween and Christmas and belongs to both holidays. The 1985 TV special Garfield's Halloween Adventure belongs here too.

arcade-golden-age.context_blurb: The arcade golden age is the roughly 1978-1983 period when standing coin-operated video-game cabinets exploded across America and Japan, becoming teenage hangouts, million-dollar fortune machines, and the real birthplace of the whole video-game industry. Atari — the California company founded by Nolan Bushnell — had kicked things off in 1972 with the paddle-and-ball cabinet Pong, but the explosion came when Taito's 1978 Space Invaders (designed by Tomohiro Nishikado) emptied Japan of 100-yen coins. Namco followed in 1980 with Toru Iwatani's maze-chomper Pac-Man, Nintendo's young designer Shigeru Miyamoto broke through in 1981 with the climbing-ape cabinet Donkey Kong, and the field filled with Namco's shooter Galaga, Williams Electronics' Defender (designed by Eugene Jarvis), Williams' twin-stick shooter Robotron: 2084 (also Jarvis) and jousting-ostrich game Joust, Atari's track-ball shooter Centipede (co-designed by Dona Bailey), Atari's vector-graphics Asteroids, Konami's Frogger, Gottlieb's cube-hopper Q*bert, Namco's Dig Dug, Stern Electronics' Berzerk, Nintendo's Popeye, Sega's Yu Suzuki-designed OutRun, and the all-cel-animated laserdisc oddity Dragon's Lair (drawn by Don Bluth, released by Cinematronics in 1983). The genre crashed in 1983 along with home consoles, but these cabinets remain the sacred heart of video-game history. If you are interested in gaming history, visiting an old-cabinet arcade museum like Funspot in Weirs Beach, New Hampshire is a bucket-list trip.

nintendo-console-games.context_blurb: The Nintendo home-console game lineup from the 1980s through the 2000s was built around the Japanese company's legendary first-party series. Nintendo's first home console was the 1983 Japanese Famicom (Family Computer), re-released in North America in 1985 as the gray Nintendo Entertainment System (NES), which single-handedly saved the American video-game business after the 1983 home-game crash. The NES launched the industry-defining Super Mario Bros. and The Legend of Zelda, both led by designer Shigeru Miyamoto, and introduced the lone bounty-hunter sci-fi series Metroid. Nintendo's handheld Game Boy followed in 1989, designed by engineer Gunpei Yokoi, and bundled the Soviet puzzle import Tetris (negotiated by Dutch businessman Henk Rogers). The 16-bit Super Nintendo (SNES) launched in 1991 with Super Mario World and later hosted Squaresoft's Chrono Trigger (1995). The Nintendo 64 arrived in 1996 with Super Mario 64, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (1998), Mario Kart 64, Super Smash Bros., and the British studio Rare's GoldenEye 007 and Perfect Dark. Pokemon Red and Blue (1996 Japan, 1998 US) made Game Freak a household name. The GameCube (2001), Wii (2006) with motion controls, and the handheld 3DS and Switch continued the line, with Smash Bros. Melee emerging as a legendary competitive scene.

sega-sony-microsoft-consoles.context_blurb: Nintendo faced rival home game consoles during the industry's 1990s-2000s expansion, each with its own defining games. Sega — the Japanese company that had dominated the arcades — launched the 16-bit Genesis in North America in 1989 under the slogan 'Genesis does what Nintendon't,' adding its new blue-hedgehog mascot Sonic in 1991, the brawler Streets of Rage, and the oddball Earthworm Jim; followed by the troubled 1995 Saturn and the beloved 1998-1999 Dreamcast (famously launched in the US on 9/9/99) with the first fully 3D Sonic Adventure. Sony entered gaming in 1994 with the gray CD-based PlayStation, which launched Capcom's horror classic Resident Evil (1996), Konami's stealth action game Metal Gear Solid (1998), Konami's atmospheric horror Silent Hill (1999), Naughty Dog's Crash Bandicoot (1996), Final Fantasy VII (1997), and Konami's reinvented exploration-based Castlevania: Symphony of the Night (1997). The follow-up PlayStation 2 (2000) became the bestselling console in history. Microsoft entered the market in 2001 with the chunky black Xbox and its launch title Halo: Combat Evolved from the Seattle studio Bungie. The British studio Core Design's Tomb Raider (1996) also defined this console era. If you are curious about where modern console gaming came from, these three generations of consoles are where almost every signature franchise alive today was first forged.

fighting-games.context_blurb: The arcade and console fighting-game explosion came in the 1990s, when two players would stand side-by-side at a cabinet and trade punches, kicks, projectiles, and finishing moves until one character fell. Capcom's Street Fighter II (1991) was the breakthrough: eight playable world warriors — the Japanese karate master Ryu and his American rival Ken, the kung-fu fighter Chun-Li, the sumo Honda, the yoga master Dhalsim, the Soviet grappler Zangief, the Brazilian Blanka, and the Air Force pilot Guile — fought in one-on-one duels with special moves triggered by specific joystick-and-button combos (like the quarter-circle-forward-and-punch fireball move Ryu throws). Midway's answer in 1992 was the bloody Mortal Kombat, developed in Chicago, using digitized real actors as the fighters and famous for its gruesome finishing moves called Fatalities. Namco (the Pac-Man studio) launched the fully 3D fighter Tekken in 1994. The genre expanded with Capcom's Super Street Fighter II Turbo (1994) and its hidden fighter Akuma (called Gouki in Japan), Midway's 1993 arcade basketball cross-over NBA Jam, and Konami's foot-pad rhythm game Dance Dance Revolution (1998). Fighting-game lore — unlockable hidden characters, cheat codes, specific joystick inputs, and tournament stories — is deep arcade canon. If you are interested in competitive gaming, fighting-game history runs straight through 1990s arcades, and the top tournament scenes for these games still thrive today at events like Evo.

king-of-kong-and-arcade-lore.context_blurb: Arcade high-score chasing has legends of its own. The core story is centered on Walter Day's arcade in a small Iowa town, which in the early 1980s became the official Twin Galaxies scorekeeper for every classic arcade cabinet in America. Day tracked player scores, verified records with Polaroids, and built the mythology around the two fiercest Donkey Kong rivals: the Florida pizza-parlor owner Billy Mitchell — who in 1982 posted the Donkey Kong record and later claimed the first-ever perfect Pac-Man score at a Funspot arcade in Weirs Beach, New Hampshire — and the Washington state high-school science teacher Steve Wiebe, who challenged him in 2003 and became famous through the 2007 Seth Gordon documentary The King of Kong: A Fistful of Quarters. Other legendary arcade lore includes Pac-Man's integer-overflow 'kill screen,' Donkey Kong's kill screen, the 'Minus World' glitch in Super Mario Bros., the Konami Code (dreamed up by Konami programmer Kazuhisa Hashimoto), the infamous Alamogordo, New Mexico desert burial of unsold Atari E.T. cartridges, the Polybius urban legend, Ms. Pac-Man's bootleg origin, and arcade cameos in The Last Starfighter (1984), WarGames (1983), Wreck-It Ralph (2012), and Stranger Things. If you want to understand what classic arcade culture felt like, that 2007 documentary is the single best place to start — it captures the whole scene better than any history book.

golden-age-comics.context_blurb: American superhero and newspaper-strip comic books ran from the industry's Golden Age (roughly 1938 to 1950) through the Bronze Age and into the Modern Age; the story here stops at about 2003. The founding titles include Action Comics #1 (June 1938), where creators Jerry Siegel and Joe Shuster introduced Superman at DC Comics; Detective Comics #27 (May 1939) where Batman debuted; the 1941 Captain America #1 by Joe Simon and Jack Kirby; the 1941 Wonder Woman by psychologist William Moulton Marston; and the 1961 Marvel Silver Age launched by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby with Fantastic Four #1, soon followed by Spider-Man (Lee and Steve Ditko, 1962), the X-Men (1963), the Hulk, Thor, Daredevil, Black Panther (1966), and Wolverine (1974). The great creator-driven storylines include Chris Claremont's long X-Men run (1975-1991), Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons's Watchmen (1986), Frank Miller's Batman: The Dark Knight Returns (1986) and Daredevil run, Neil Gaiman's Sandman (1989-1996), Mike Mignola's Hellboy (1994), Garth Ennis's Preacher and Punisher MAX, Jeff Smith's self-published Bone (1991-2004), Mark Millar's Kick-Ass (2008), and newspaper strips like Bill Watterson's Calvin and Hobbes, Herge's Belgian Tintin, Berkeley Breathed's Bloom County, Hal Foster's Prince Valiant, and Lee Falk's The Phantom.
